questions.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
questions.q: Page 218 defines bronchiectasis as abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchi (initially medium sized, later the entire bronchial tree) plus ______ fibrosis of bronchioles.
opts: Interstitial
Subpleural
Peribronchial
Obliterative
questions.exp: The definition joins 'Abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchi (Initially medium sized → entire bronchial tree)' with 'Obliterative fibrosis of bronchioles → Obstructive lung disease (can have restrictive component)'. The bronchiolar fibrosis explains the mixed obstructive-restrictive physiology. (Book p218)

questions.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
questions.q: How does the page 218 note define pseudobronchiectasis, and which two infections are named?
opts: Reversible dilatation of bronchi following infection — influenza and COVID
Reversible dilatation of bronchioles following obstruction — tuberculosis and measles
Irreversible dilatation of bronchioles following infection — influenza and COVID
Reversible dilatation of bronchi following fibrosis — influenza and tuberculosis
questions.exp: The note reads 'Pseudobronchiectasis : Reversible dilatation of bronchi following infection (Influenza, COVID).' Reversibility is what separates it from the irreversible disease defined in the opening line. (Book p218)

questions.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about how bronchiectasis is classified on page 218.
opts: False — it is listed among the restrictive lung diseases with no obstructive component
True — it is listed among the obstructive lung diseases and the definition adds that it can have a restrictive component
False — it is listed as a purely vascular lung disease
True — it is listed among the obstructive diseases but can never have a restrictive component
questions.exp: The definition ends '→ Obstructive lung disease (can have restrictive component)', and the list of obstructive diseases places bronchiectasis at item d, after COPD, bronchial asthma and bronchiolitis. Both the obstructive label and the possible restrictive component are printed. (Book p218)

questions.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
questions.q: Which sequence does the page 218 pathogenesis flowchart print after the initial infective insult?
opts: Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → inflammation → cartilage hypertrophy → abnormal and reversible dilatation of bronchi
Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → inflammation → goblet cell hyperplasia → loss of smooth muscle → abnormal dilatation
Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → inflammation → loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in bronchi → abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchi
Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → fibrosis → loss of cilia → abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchioles
questions.exp: The flowchart runs 'Initial insult : Infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic' → 'Inflammation' → 'Loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in bronchi (Bronchi & bronchiole both have smooth muscle)' → 'Abnormal & irreversible dilatation of bronchi'. Goblet cell hyperplasia sits on the separate mucus limb of the chart. (Book p218)

questions.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
questions.q: The flowchart parenthesises a fact about smooth muscle in the airways. Which statement is printed?
opts: Only bronchi have smooth muscle, bronchioles do not
Only bronchioles have smooth muscle, bronchi do not
Neither bronchi nor bronchioles have smooth muscle; only the trachea does
Bronchi and bronchioles both have smooth muscle
questions.exp: The bracket after 'Loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in bronchi' reads '(Bronchi & bronchiole both have smooth muscle)'. This contrasts with cartilage, which is lost at bronchiolar level and is discussed later in the chapter's treatment rationale. (Book p218)

questions.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
questions.q: The mucus limb of the page 218 flowchart runs through three steps. Which sequence is printed?
opts: Mucous gland hyperplasia → serous secretion → bronchospasm
Goblet cell atrophy → mucus inspissation → dilatation of airway
Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → obstruction of airway
Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → loss of cilia
questions.exp: One arrow of the chart reads '3. Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → Obstruction of airway.' Loss of cilia is a separate numbered step (1) with its own downstream consequence, pooling of secretion. (Book p218)

questions.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
questions.q: Which chain is printed as step 1 on the left of the page 218 flowchart?
opts: Loss of goblet cells → loss of mucociliary escalator → pooling of secretion
Loss of cilia → loss of mucociliary escalator mechanism → pooling of secretion in airway
Loss of cilia → mucus hypersecretion → obstruction of airway
Loss of cartilage → airway collapse → pooling of secretion in airway
questions.exp: Step 1 reads 'Loss of cilia → loss of micro ciliary escalator mechanism → pooling of secretion in airway', and the pooled secretion loops back into 'microbial colonisation leading to infusion' and inflammation. Cartilage loss is not part of this first step. (Book p218)

questions.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
questions.q: Match each numbered or arrowed step of the page 218 flowchart with its printed text — 1) Step 1 2) Step 2 3) Step 3 4) Arrow back into inflammation … A) Weakening & inflammation of bronchial wall B) Loss of cilia → loss of mucociliary escalator → pooling of secretion C) Microbial colonisation leading to infusion D) Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → obstruction of airway
questions.exp: The flowchart numbers '1. Loss of cilia → loss of micro ciliary escalator mechanism → pooling of secretion in airway', '2. weakening & inflammation of bronchial wall' and '3. Goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → Obstruction of airway', and the closed arrow returning to inflammation reads 'microbial colonisation leading to infusion'. (Book p218)

questions.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
questions.q: Match each morphological type with the letter used in the page 219 grades figure — 1) Cylindrical/tubular 2) Varicose 3) Saccular/cystic … A) S B) C C) V
questions.exp: The caption reads 'A normal bronchus (N) compared with the three grades of severity of bronchiectasis: cylindrical (C), varicose (V), and saccular (cystic) (S)'. The letters C, V and S follow the severity order shown. (Book p219)

questions.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
questions.q: The page 219 note on traction bronchiectasis links it to fibrosis and to a classification. Which statement is printed?
opts: Traction bronchiectasis → elastolysis (restrictive type: classified under ILD)
Traction bronchiectasis → fibrosis (restrictive type: classified under ILD)
Traction bronchiectasis → fibrosis (obstructive type: classified under COPD)
Traction bronchiectasis → atelectasis (mixed type: classified under bronchiectasis)
questions.exp: The note reads 'Traction bronchiectasis → Fibrosis (Restrictive type : Classified under ILD).' The dilatation is pulled open by surrounding fibrotic contraction, so the physiology is restrictive rather than obstructive. (Book p219)

questions.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
questions.q: Which epidemiological details are printed in the page 219 note?
opts: Usually unilateral, most common lobe the left lower lobe, F > M, 20–40 yrs
Usually unilateral, most common lobe the left upper lobe, M > F, 50–70 yrs
Usually bilateral, most common lobe the right middle lobe, M > F, 20–40 yrs
Usually unilateral, most common lobe the left lower lobe, F > M, 50–70 yrs
questions.exp: The note reads 'Bronchiectasis : usually unilateral (can become bilateral)', 'm/c lobe involved : Left lower lobe', 'F > m' and '50 – 70 yrs'. The right middle lobe is the site of Brock's syndrome on page 220, not the overall commonest lobe. (Book p219)

questions.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
questions.q: TRUE or FALSE about the laterality of bronchiectasis printed on page 219.
opts: True — it is usually unilateral but can become bilateral
True — the left lower lobe is spared because of its longer bronchus
False — it is always bilateral by definition
False — it is always unilateral and never becomes bilateral
questions.exp: The note says 'usually unilateral (can become bilateral)'. It also names the left lower lobe as the commonest lobe involved, so the left lower lobe is the most, not the least, affected site. (Book p219)

questions.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
questions.q: Match each histological panel caption with its letter on page 219 — 1) Fibrosis and cartilage destruction 2) Mucosal and mucous gland hyperplasia 3) Excessive mucus and exudate 4) Inflammatory cell infiltrate … A) b B) d C) a D) c
questions.exp: The four panels are captioned 'a. Fibrosis and cartilage destruction', 'b. mucosal and mucous gland hyperplasia', 'c. Excessive mucus and exudate' and 'd. Inflammatory cell infiltrate'. Cartilage destruction is what allows the airway to dilate irreversibly. (Book p219)

questions.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
questions.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis has dilated bronchi within the fibrotic zone on CT. How does page 219 classify this?
opts: Traction bronchiectasis, an obstructive type classified under COPD
Traction bronchiectasis, a restrictive type classified under ILD
Saccular bronchiectasis, a cystic type requiring resection
Pseudobronchiectasis, a reversible post-infective dilatation
questions.exp: Page 219 prints 'Traction bronchiectasis → Fibrosis (Restrictive type : Classified under ILD)'. The dilatation is part of the fibrotic process rather than a primary infective airway disease, which is why it is filed under ILD. (Book p219)

questions.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
questions.q: Three morphological types of dilatation are shown on page 219. Which list is printed?
opts: Varicose, saccular and beaded
Tubular, moniliform and cystic
Cylindrical/tubular, varicose and cystic
Cylindrical/tubular, saccular and fusiform
questions.exp: The three labelled drawings read 'Cylindrical / tubular', 'Varicose' and 'Cystic', with the figure caption adding 'saccular (cystic) (S)'. Fusiform, beaded and moniliform are not printed here. (Book p219)

questions.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
questions.q: Match each named paediatric syndrome with its printed abnormality — 1) Mounier-Kuhn 2) William Campbell 3) Kartagener's syndrome 4) Young's syndrome … A) Azoospermia causing infertility B) Tracheobronchomegaly C) Primary ciliary dyskinesia D) Absence of cartilage
questions.exp: The list reads 'Mounier Kuhn : Tracheobronchomegaly', 'William Campbell : Absence of cartilage', 'Kartagener's syndrome : Primary ciliary dyskinesia' and 'Young's syndrome : Azoospermia → Infertility'. Mounier-Kuhn enlarges the airway while William Campbell weakens it through missing cartilage. (Book p220)

questions.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
questions.q: Which triad does page 220 print for Kartagener's syndrome?
opts: Bronchiectasis, sinusitis and situs inversus
Sinusitis, situs inversus and yellow nails
Bronchiectasis, sinusitis and azoospermia
Bronchiectasis, situs inversus and azoospermia
questions.exp: The page reads 'Kartagener's syndrome : Primary ciliary dyskinesia (bronchiectasis, sinusitis & situs inversus)'. Azoospermia belongs to Young's syndrome, which sits immediately below it on the same list. (Book p220)

questions.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
questions.q: Three conditions are bracketed on page 220 as causing impaired mucociliary clearance. Which three are printed?
opts: Kartagener's syndrome, cystic fibrosis and yellow nail syndrome
Kartagener's syndrome, Young's syndrome and α1-antitrypsin deficiency
Kartagener's syndrome, cystic fibrosis and Young's syndrome
Cystic fibrosis, Young's syndrome and isolated IgA deficiency
questions.exp: The note reads 'Impaired mucociliary clearance : Kartageners syndrome. Cystic fibrosis. Young's syndrome.' Yellow nail syndrome and α1-antitrypsin deficiency appear in the paediatric list above but not in the clearance bracket. (Book p220)

questions.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
questions.q: What does page 220 say about isolated IgA deficiency?
opts: It is the least common primary immunodeficiency
It is the most common secondary immunodeficiency
It is the commonest cause of bronchiectasis in adults
It is the most common primary immunodeficiency
questions.exp: The note reads 'Isolated IgA deficiency : m/c primary immunodeficiency', and the adult list repeats 'Immunodeficiency (Also seen in childhood) : IgA deficiency (m/c)'. It is a predisposing cause, not the commonest overall cause of adult bronchiectasis. (Book p220)

questions.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
questions.q: Obliterative bronchiectasis due to infection in childhood is called ______ syndrome on page 220.
opts: Brock
McLeod
Kartagener
Swyer-James
questions.exp: The note reads 'Obliterative bronchiectasis d/t infection in childhood : mcleod's syndrome.' Brock's syndrome, printed lower on the same page, is a different entity — secondary lymphadenopathy causing right middle lobe bronchiectasis. (Book p220)

questions.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
questions.q: The adult aetiology list gives two percentages. Which pair is printed?
opts: Idiopathic 60%, post-infection mostly TB 20%
Idiopathic 40%, post-infection mostly TB 30%
Idiopathic 30%, post-infection mostly pertussis 40%
Idiopathic 30%, post-infection mostly TB 40%
questions.exp: The adult list reads 'Idiopathic : 30%' and 'Post-infection : mostly TB (40%)', with mechanical obstruction, immunodeficiency and autoimmune causes below them. TB dominates the adult post-infective group even though pertussis and measles dominate the paediatric one. (Book p220)

questions.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
questions.q: A patient with right middle lobe bronchiectasis is found to have enlarged hilar nodes compressing the lobar bronchus. Which eponym does page 220 print?
opts: McLeod's syndrome — obliterative bronchiectasis after childhood infection
Brock's syndrome — secondary lymphadenopathy causing right middle lobe bronchiectasis
William Campbell syndrome — absence of cartilage
Mounier-Kuhn syndrome — tracheobronchomegaly
questions.exp: The adult mechanical-obstruction line reads 'Brock's syndrome : Secondary lymphadenopathy → Right middle lobe bronchiectasis'. The obstruction is extrinsic compression, not a primary airway wall defect. (Book p220)

questions.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — three of these appear in the paediatric aetiology list of page 220, one does not:
opts: α1-antitrypsin deficiency
Yellow nail syndrome
Sjögren syndrome
Cystic fibrosis
questions.exp: The paediatric list contains pertussis/measles, the syndromes, cystic fibrosis, yellow nail syndrome and α1-antitrypsin deficiency. Sjögren syndrome is the autoimmune entry in the ADULT list at the foot of the page. (Book p220)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: Which description of sputum is printed under the symptoms on page 221?
opts: Copious, foul smelling, three layered (mucus, mucopurulent, pus) with early morning exacerbation
Copious, odourless, four layered (mucus, mucopurulent, pus, blood) with early morning exacerbation
Copious, foul smelling, three layered (mucus, mucopurulent, pus) with evening exacerbation
Scanty, odourless, two layered (mucus, pus) with evening exacerbation
questions.exp: The sputum sub-list reads 'Copius', 'Foul smelling', '3 layered : mucus, mucopurulent, pus' and 'early morning exacerbation'. The layering reflects the settling of different densities of secretions overnight. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: How does page 221 explain haemoptysis in bronchiectasis?
opts: Due to erosion of granulation tissue into the pulmonary artery
Due to rupture of a thin walled vein on the bronchial wall
Due to bronchial artery hypertrophy from chronic inflammation
Due to rupture of a thin walled artery on the bronchial wall
questions.exp: The line reads 'Hemoptysis : d/t rupture of thin walled vein on bronchial wall.' The vessel named is a vein, not an artery or granulation tissue. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: Which auscultatory findings are printed, and in which type is clubbing described?
opts: Early and mid inspiratory coarse crackles with diffuse rhonchi; clubbing in adults, seen in the cylindrical type
Late inspiratory fine crackles with a pleural rub; clubbing in adults, seen in the varicose type
Early and mid inspiratory coarse crackles with diffuse rhonchi; clubbing in children, seen in the cystic type
Expiratory wheeze with diffuse rhonchi; clubbing in children, seen in the varicose type
questions.exp: The findings read 'Clubbing in children (seen in cystic type)', then 'Early and mid inspiratory coarse crackles' and 'Diffuse rhonchi'. Coarse early-mid inspiratory crackles differ from the fine bibasal inspiratory crackles of fibrosis. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: The page 221 note ties allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis to a specific bronchiectasis pattern. Which description is printed?
opts: Central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l), which can go with interstitial lung disease
Central, distal, upper lobe bronchiectasis (usually unilateral), which can go with asthma only
Central, proximal, lower lobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l), which can go with emphysema
Peripheral, distal, lower lobe bronchiectasis (usually unilateral), which can go with COPD
questions.exp: The note reads 'Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillius : Central, proximal, upperlobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l); Can go with interstitial lung disease (ILD).' The central-proximal distribution follows the larger airways colonised by Aspergillus. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: The clinical-features section advises: 'always rule out bronchiectasis in recurrent ______.'
opts: Sinusitis
Haemoptysis
Asthma
Pneumonia
questions.exp: The line reads 'Acute exacerbation d/t infection : Always rule out bronchiectasis in recurrent pneumonia.' Recurrent infection in the same segment is the clinical clue to an underlying dilated, poorly cleared airway. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: Match each plain-film sign with its printed description — 1) Tram track sign 2) Bunch of grape appearance 3) Finger in glove appearance … A) Due to mucus inside B) Dilated airways with lack of tapering C) Clustered cystic spaces
questions.exp: The film is captioned 'Tram track sign (Dilated airways with lack of tapering)', 'Bunch of grape appearance' and 'Finger in glove appearance (d/t mucus inside)'. Loss of tapering is the radiographic signature of the dilated airway. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: Which three criteria for the CT diagnosis are printed under 'Volumetric multidetector helical CT scan : IOC'?
opts: Airway dilatation (1–1.5 times the adjacent vessels), lack of bronchial tapering, and tree-in-bud opacity (non-specific) from endobronchial obstruction giving nodules plus signet ring
Airway dilatation (1–1.5 times the adjacent vessels), lack of bronchial tapering, and honeycombing with traction Bronchiectasis
Airway narrowing (less than the adjacent vessels), lack of bronchial tapering, and tree-in-bud opacity
Airway dilatation (2–3 times the adjacent vessels), preserved bronchial tapering, and tree-in-bud opacity
questions.exp: The three CT criteria read '1. Airway dilatation (1–1.5 times than adjacent vessels). 2. Lack of bronchial tapering. 3. Tree in bud opacity (Non-specific) : endobronchial obstruction → nodules + signet ring.' The ratio compares the airway with its adjacent vessel, not with a fixed diameter. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: A young asthmatic with poorly controlled disease has central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis on CT, and a background of interstitial lung disease is suspected. Which page 221 note applies?
opts: Sicca bronchiectasis — central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis seen with haemoptysis and cough
Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis — central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l), which can go with ILD
Brock's syndrome — central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis from secondary lymphadenopathy
Traction bronchiectasis — central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis classified under ILD
questions.exp: The note reads 'Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillius : Central, proximal, upperlobe bronchiectasis (usually b/l)' and 'Can go with interstitial lung disease (ILD)'. Sicca bronchiectasis, printed just above, is the TB-associated pattern with haemoptysis and cough. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
questions.q: The chest X-ray in bronchiectasis is introduced on page 221 with a single qualifier: 'X-Ray : ______ sensitivity'.
opts: High
Variable
Intermediate
Low
questions.exp: The line reads 'X-Ray : Low sensitivity', which is why the volumetric multidetector helical CT scan is designated the IOC on the same page despite the classic tram track, bunch of grape and finger-in-glove signs. (Book p221)

questions.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
questions.q: Match each complication with its printed qualifier — 1) Massive haemoptysis 2) Empyema 3) Secondary amyloidosis 4) Lung abscess … A) With bronchopleural fistula B) AA type C) Especially in dry bronchiectasis D) Listed without a qualifier
questions.exp: The complication list reads '1. Cor pulmonale. 2. massive hemoptysis : especially in dry bronchiectasis. 3. Empyema with bronchopleural fistula. 4. Secondary Amyloidosis (AA). 5. Lung Abscess.' Dry bronchiectasis is the variant that bleeds rather than expectorates. (Book p222)

questions.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
questions.q: Cor pulmonale is split on page 222 into acute and chronic types. Which two causes are printed?
opts: Acute: most common cause lung parenchymal disease; chronic: due to thromboembolism
Acute: most common cause thromboembolism; chronic: due to left heart disease
Acute: most common cause thromboembolism; chronic: due to lung parenchymal disease such as ILD, chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis
Acute: most common cause pneumonia; chronic: due to ILD, chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis
questions.exp: The note reads 'Cor pulmonale : RV dilatation/hypertrophy +/− RV Failure' and then 'Types → Acute (m/c cause : thromboembolism)' and '→ Chronic (d/t lung parenchymal disease : ILD, chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis)'. Acute cor pulmonale is embolic; chronic is parenchymal. (Book p222)

questions.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
questions.q: Which concentration of nebulised hypertonic saline is printed under airway clearance on page 222?
opts: 7% sodium bicarbonate
7% hypertonic saline
3% hypertonic saline
0.9% normal saline
questions.exp: The airway-clearance line reads 'Nebulized 7% hypertonic saline, Steam inhalation, flutter valves', together with postural drainage. Hypertonic saline is used to osmotically draw water into secretions and make them easier to clear. (Book p222)

questions.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
questions.q: Match each therapy with the role printed against it on page 222 — 1) Recombinant human DNase 2) Nebulized gentamycin 3) Nebulized 7% hypertonic saline … A) As prophylaxis B) Airway clearance agent C) Listed first among CF-associated therapies
questions.exp: Under 'CF associated bronchiectasis' the page prints 'Recombinant human DNase' then 'Nebulized gentamycin as prophylaxis'. The 7% hypertonic saline belongs to the mainstay airway-clearance list above. The DNase thins DNA-rich secretions while the aminoglycoside suppresses chronic Pseudomonas. (Book p222)

questions.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
questions.q: Macrolides have two roles in the page 222 treatment block. Which statement is printed?
opts: They do not reach effective lung concentrations, but have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 6–9 months
They reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa, and have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 3–6 months
They reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa, and have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 6–9 months
They reach effective concentration only in serum, and have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 6–9 months
questions.exp: The antibiotic block reads 'macrolides & penicillin (Beta-lactams) : Reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa' and 'macrolides : immunomodulatory action - recommended for 6–9 months'. Both the penetration and the 6–9 month duration are printed. (Book p222)

questions.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
questions.q: Which organism hierarchy is printed in the closing note on page 222?
opts: Pseudomonas > S. pneumoniae >> H. influenzae
H. influenzae >> Pseudomonas > S. pneumoniae
S. pneumoniae >> H. influenzae > Pseudomonas
Pseudomonas >> H. influenzae > S. pneumoniae
questions.exp: The note reads 'Organism infecting & weakening bronchial wall → Pseudomonas >> H. influenzae > S. pneumoniae.' The double arrow marks Pseudomonas as the dominant organism in damaged airways. (Book p222)

units.title: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
units.sec: Definition (Irreversible Dilatation Plus Obliterative Bronchiolar Fibrosis), Pseudobronchiectasis, the Obstructive-Disease List, Pathogenesis Flowchart and the Normal-vs-Bronchiectasis Diagram
units.guide:
Bronchiectasis (p218) is abnormal and irreversible dilatation of bronchi — initially medium sized, later the entire bronchial tree — plus obliterative fibrosis of bronchioles, producing obstructive lung disease that can have a restrictive component. Pseudobronchiectasis is the reversible dilatation that follows influenza or COVID.
It is listed among the obstructive diseases with COPD (emphysema, bronchitis, small airway disease), bronchial asthma, bronchiolitis and cystic fibrosis.
Pathogenesis: infection (mostly TB)/idiopathic → inflammation → loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in bronchi (bronchi and bronchioles both have smooth muscle) → abnormal and irreversible dilatation; the mucus limb runs goblet cell hyperplasia → mucus hypersecretion → airway obstruction, while loss of cilia removes the mucociliary escalator and pools secretions, feeding microbial colonisation and further inflammation. The diagram contrasts a normal bronchus (outer wall, cilia, mucus, mucous gland) with loss of cilia, increased mucus and destruction of the wall.

units.title: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
units.sec: Types of Dilatation (Cylindrical/Varicose/Cystic), Traction Bronchiectasis, Lobe/Sex/Age Distribution and the Four Histological Features
units.guide:
Types of dilatation (p219) are cylindrical/tubular, varicose and cystic, drawn against a normal bronchus (N) as grades C, V and S, with a CT showing cystic changes at the upper lobe. Traction bronchiectasis follows fibrosis and is a restrictive type classified under ILD.
Distribution: usually unilateral though it can become bilateral, most common lobe the left lower lobe, F > M, age 50–70 years.
Histology: fibrosis and cartilage destruction; mucosal and mucous gland hyperplasia; excessive mucus and exudate; inflammatory cell infiltrate.

units.title: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
units.sec: Paediatric Aetiology (Post-Infective, Mounier-Kuhn, William Campbell, Kartagener, Young, Yellow Nail, α1-Antitrypsin), Impaired Mucociliary Clearance, McLeod, IgA Deficiency and Adult Aetiology
units.guide:
Paediatric aetiology (p220): post-infective pertussis and measles; syndromes usually cystic in the upper to mid fields — Mounier-Kuhn (tracheobronchomegaly), William Campbell (absence of cartilage), Kartagener's (primary ciliary dyskinesia with bronchiectasis, sinusitis and situs inversus), Young's (azoospermia causing infertility); cystic fibrosis; yellow nail syndrome; α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
Impaired mucociliary clearance is bracketed for Kartagener's, cystic fibrosis and Young's syndrome. Obliterative bronchiectasis after childhood infection is McLeod's syndrome, and isolated IgA deficiency is the commonest primary immunodeficiency.
Adult causes: idiopathic 30%, post-infection mostly TB 40%, mechanical obstruction such as Brock's syndrome (secondary lymphadenopathy causing right middle lobe bronchiectasis), immunodeficiency (IgA deficiency commonest) and autoimmune disease such as Sjögren syndrome.

units.title: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
units.sec: Clinical Features (Three-Layered Sputum, Postural Cough, Haemoptysis Mechanism), Examination Findings, Sicca/ABPA Notes, Plain-Film Signs and the Three CT Criteria
units.guide:
Clinical features (p221): chronic cough with postural variation; copious foul-smelling sputum in three layers — mucus, mucopurulent, pus — with early morning exacerbation; haemoptysis from rupture of a thin-walled vein on the bronchial wall; exacerbations from infection, and bronchiectasis must always be excluded in recurrent pneumonia.
Findings: clubbing in children, seen in the cystic type; early and mid inspiratory coarse crackles with diffuse rhonchi. Note sicca bronchiectasis with haemoptysis and cough points to TB, and ABPA gives central, proximal, upper lobe bronchiectasis, usually bilateral, which can accompany ILD.
X-ray has low sensitivity but shows the tram track sign (dilated airways with lack of tapering), bunch of grape appearance and finger-in-glove appearance from mucus inside. Volumetric multidetector helical CT is the IOC: airway dilatation 1–1.5 times the adjacent vessels, lack of bronchial tapering, and tree-in-bud opacity (non-specific) from endobronchial obstruction giving nodules plus signet ring.

units.title: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
units.sec: Complications (Cor Pulmonale, Massive Haemoptysis, Empyema, Amyloidosis, Abscess), Airway Clearance and CF Therapies, Surgery, Antibiotic Rationale, Macrolide Duration and the Infecting-Organism Hierarchy
units.guide:
Complications (p222): cor pulmonale; massive haemoptysis, especially in dry bronchiectasis; empyema with bronchopleural fistula; secondary amyloidosis (AA); lung abscess. Cor pulmonale is RV dilatation/hypertrophy ± failure, acute from thromboembolism and chronic from parenchymal disease such as ILD, chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis.
Treatment: mainstay is airway clearance with nebulised 7% hypertonic saline, steam inhalation, flutter valves and postural drainage; CF-associated disease gets recombinant human DNase and nebulised gentamycin as prophylaxis; surgery is localized resection for localized disease.
Antibiotics: macrolides and penicillin (beta-lactams) reach effective concentration within lung and bronchial mucosa, and macrolides have an immunomodulatory action recommended for 6–9 months. The organism hierarchy that infects and weakens the bronchial wall is Pseudomonas >> H. influenzae > S. pneumoniae.
